items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The rule u′ = u − v for the velocity of an object measured in a frame moving at v"?
items.answer: Galilean velocity addition
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of Galilean velocity addition.

items.stem: A student claims: "Observers in different inertial frames always agree on the velocity of an object." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Velocity depends on the frame (u′ = u − v); they agree on acceleration in Galilean relativity, not velocity.
items.markingKey: Velocity depends on the frame (u′ = u − v); they agree on acceleration in Galilean relativity, not velocity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a non-inertial frame and an inertial frame.
items.answer: In an inertial frame (not accelerating) Newton’s laws hold without fictitious forces; in a non-inertial (accelerating or rotating) frame, apparent forces such as centrifugal force must be introduced.
items.markingKey: In an inertial frame (not accelerating) Newton’s laws hold without fictitious forces; in a non-inertial (accelerating or rotating) frame, apparent forces such as centrifugal force must be introduced. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Chloé walks towards the back of a train at 1.5 m s⁻¹ relative to the train, which moves at 20 m s⁻¹ along a track near Singapore. Use the Galilean transformation to find her velocity relative to the track.
items.markingKey: u = u′ + v (M1) = 18.5 m s⁻¹ in the direction of the train (A1).

items.stem: Hana walks towards the front of a train at 1.2 m s⁻¹ relative to the train, which moves at 30 m s⁻¹ along a track near Cape Town. Use the Galilean transformation to find her velocity relative to the track.
items.markingKey: D. u = u′ + v (M1) = 31.2 m s⁻¹ in the direction of the train (A1).

items.stem: A boat crosses a river 120 m wide. It moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ relative to the water, heading straight across, and the river flows at 3.0 m s⁻¹. (a) Use Galilean velocity addition to find the boat’s velocity relative to the bank. (b) Calculate the crossing time. (c) Determine the distance downstream at which it lands. (d) Explain why light does not behave in this way.
items.answer: (a) 5.0 m s⁻¹ at 36.9° downstream from straight across; (b) 30 s; (c) 90 m; (d) the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all inertial observers, so velocities do not add in the Galilean way at relativistic speeds.
items.markingKey: (a) 5.0 m s⁻¹ at 36.9° downstream from straight across; (b) 30 s; (c) 90 m; (d) the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all inertial observers, so velocities do not add in the Galilean way at relativistic speeds.

items.stem: Define the term "Galilean velocity addition".
items.answer: The rule u′ = u − v for the velocity of an object measured in a frame moving at v

items.answer: acceleration
items.markingKey: B. Uniform relative motion does not change a.

items.stem: Explain why the result of the Michelson–Morley experiment was surprising in the 19th century.
items.answer: Physicists expected Earth’s motion through the ether to change the speed of light in different directions and shift the interference fringes; no shift was observed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Physicists expected Earth’s motion through the ether to change the speed of light in different directions and shift the interference fringes; no shift was observed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of the following statements about reference frames and Galilean transformations is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Sofia.)
options: No forces are involved; different inertial frames measure different lengths because they disagree on simultaneity of the end-point measurements.
Any frame moving at constant velocity is inertial; there is no experiment that distinguishes rest from uniform motion.
With ct vertical, a steeper worldline means a smaller x per ct, i.e. a slower object; a vertical line is at rest.
Galilean relativity is wrong and should not be used.
items.answer: Galilean relativity is wrong and should not be used.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: It is an excellent approximation when speeds are much smaller than c, and it is the low-speed limit of special relativity.

items.stem: An event occurs at x = 800 m, t = 15 s in frame S. Frame S′ moves at 10 m s⁻¹ along +x, with origins coinciding at t = 0. Using the Galilean transformation, calculate x′.
"An inertial frame must be at rest." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Any frame moving at constant velocity is inertial; there is no experiment that distinguishes rest from uniform motion.
items.markingKey: Any frame moving at constant velocity is inertial; there is no experiment that distinguishes rest from uniform motion. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A car travels at 35 m s⁻¹ east and a truck at 22 m s⁻¹ west on the same road. Calculate the velocity of the truck relative to the car (Galilean).
items.markingKey: D. Relative velocity = u − v = −22 − 35 (M1) = 57 m s⁻¹ westward (A1).

items.stem: "The null result of the Michelson–Morley experiment proved that the ether does not exist." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It strongly undermined the ether, but the case was settled by Einstein’s simpler, more predictive theory rather than by one experiment (NOS: theory choice and parsimony).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no fringe shift was observed to high precision; it supported the constancy of light speed. Arguments against: physicists proposed alternatives such as ether drag and Lorentz–FitzGerald contraction; a null result alone cannot prove non-existence; acceptance came when special relativity explained many results more simply. Supported judgement: It strongly undermined the ether, but the case was settled by Einstein’s simpler, more predictive theory rather than by one experiment (NOS: theory choice and parsimony). Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) by which time intervals dilate and lengths contract, always ≥ 1"?
items.answer: Lorentz factor
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of Lorentz factor.

items.stem: Aiko and a classmate in Geneva disagree about postulates of special relativity and Lorentz transformations. Which statement is correct?
options: An astronaut travelling fast feels time pass slowly on board.
An inertial frame must be at rest.
A moving clock really breaks and runs slow.
The speed of light in vacuum is one of the few absolutes: it is the same for all inertial observers, which is the second postulate.
items.answer: The speed of light in vacuum is one of the few absolutes: it is the same for all inertial observers, which is the second postulate.
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. The speed of light in vacuum is one of the few absolutes: it is the same for all inertial observers, which is the second postulate.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Galilean transformation and the Lorentz transformation.
items.answer: The Galilean transformation assumes absolute time (t′ = t) and adds velocities simply; the Lorentz transformation keeps c invariant, mixes space and time (t′ = γ(t − vx/c²)) and reduces to the Galilean form when v ≪ c.
items.markingKey: The Galilean transformation assumes absolute time (t′ = t) and adds velocities simply; the Lorentz transformation keeps c invariant, mixes space and time (t′ = γ(t − vx/c²)) and reduces to the Galilean form when v ≪ c. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Two lamps 1500 m apart flash simultaneously in the laboratory frame. Calculate the time interval between the flashes measured by an observer moving at 0.6c along the line joining them.
items.markingKey: Δt′ = γ(Δt − vΔx/c²) with Δt = 0 (M1); |Δt′| = γvΔx/c² = 3.75 μs (A1).

items.stem: "Relativistic effects only appear because clocks are badly made." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Time dilation and simultaneity are properties of space-time itself, verified with atomic clocks, muons and GPS.
items.markingKey: Time dilation and simultaneity are properties of space-time itself, verified with atomic clocks, muons and GPS. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In frame S, event A occurs at x = 0, t = 0 and event B at x = 900 m, t = 2.0 μs. Frame S′ moves at 0.60c along +x, with origins coinciding at t = 0. (a) Calculate γ. (b) Use the Lorentz transformation to find x′ and t′ for event B. (c) Determine the time interval between A and B in S′. (d) Comment on the order of the events in the two frames.
items.answer: (a) 1.25; (b) x′ = 1.25(900 − 0.6 × 3 × 10⁸ × 2 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.25 × 540 = 675 m; t′ = 1.25(2.0 × 10⁻⁶ − 0.6 × 900/3 × 10⁸) = 1.25(2.0 − 1.8) μs = 0.25 μs; (c) 0.25 μs; (d) B is still after A in S′ but much closer in time; because the interval is timelike (c²t² > x²) the order cannot be reversed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1.25; (b) x′ = 1.25(900 − 0.6 × 3 × 10⁸ × 2 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.25 × 540 = 675 m; t′ = 1.25(2.0 × 10⁻⁶ − 0.6 × 900/3 × 10⁸) = 1.25(2.0 − 1.8) μs = 0.25 μs; (c) 0.25 μs; (d) B is still after A in S′ but much closer in time; because the interval is timelike (c²t² > x²) the order cannot be reversed.

items.stem: Define the term "relativity of simultaneity".
items.answer: Events that are simultaneous in one inertial frame are generally not simultaneous in another frame moving relative to it
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: events that are simultaneous in one inertial frame are generally not simultaneous in another frame moving relative to it. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: As a spacecraft’s speed increases towards c, γ
items.answer: increases without limit

items.stem: Explain, using the relativity of simultaneity, why "now" is not the same for all observers.
items.answer: From t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), events at different x with equal t have different t′; whether two distant events happen at the same time depends on the observer’s frame.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: From t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), events at different x with equal t have different t′; whether two distant events happen at the same time depends on the observer’s frame. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An observer in frame S sees two events happen at the same place and the same time. An observer in any other inertial frame
options: may see them in reverse order
also sees them happen at the same place and time
items.answer: also sees them happen at the same place and time
items.markingKey: B. A single space-time point is the same event.

items.stem:
This question is about postulates of special relativity and Lorentz transformations.

(a) In frame S an event occurs at x = 1200 m, t = 1.0 μs. Frame S′ moves at 0.98c along +x, with origins coinciding at t = 0. Calculate x′ for the event. [2]

(b) Explain, using the relativity of simultaneity, why "now" is not the same for all observers. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Einstein’s special relativity was accepted because of the Michelson–Morley experiment." [4]
items.answer: (a) 4550 m (b) From t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), events at different x with equal t have different t′; whether two distant events happen at the same time depends on the observer’s frame. (c) The theory was built mainly on theoretical consistency and was accepted after many confirmations; the experiment was supporting evidence rather than the direct cause (NOS).
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] x′ = γ(x − vt) (M1) = 5.03(1200 − 294) = 4550 m (A1). (b) [3 marks] From t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), events at different x with equal t have different t′; whether two distant events happen at the same time depends on the observer’s frame. (c) [4 marks] For: the null result is consistent with the invariance of c. Against: Einstein said the experiment had little influence on his thinking; he was motivated by the symmetry of Maxwell’s equations; acceptance followed confirmation by later experiments (time dilation of muons, particle accelerators). Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The theory was built mainly on theoretical consistency and was accepted after many confirmations; the experiment was supporting evidence rather than the direct cause (NOS).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "length contraction"?
options: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames
A graph with ct on the vertical axis and x on the horizontal axis on which events are points and objects follow worldlines
A coordinate system with clocks and rulers from which observers measure the positions and times of events
The shortening of a length along the direction of motion measured by an observer moving relative to the object, L = L₀/γ
items.answer: The shortening of a length along the direction of motion measured by an observer moving relative to the object, L = L₀/γ
items.markingKey: D. "length contraction" is the shortening of a length along the direction of motion measured by an observer moving relative to the object, L = L₀/γ.

items.stem: Explain the difference between dilated time and proper time.
items.answer: Proper time is measured in the frame where the events are at the same place (the shortest interval); dilated time Δt = γΔt₀ is measured by an observer for whom the events are at different places.
items.markingKey: Proper time is measured in the frame where the events are at the same place (the shortest interval); dilated time Δt = γΔt₀ is measured by an observer for whom the events are at different places. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An astronaut moving at 0.8c relative to Earth measures her heartbeat. Compared with Earth-based measurements of her heartbeat, she measures
items.answer: a shorter period
items.markingKey: D. She measures proper time; Earth sees dilated intervals.

items.stem: A student claims: "An astronaut travelling fast feels time pass slowly on board." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: In her own frame everything is normal: her heartbeat and clocks run at the usual rate; it is the observer in another frame who measures her clocks running slow.
items.markingKey: In her own frame everything is normal: her heartbeat and clocks run at the usual rate; it is the observer in another frame who measures her clocks running slow. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Muons with a mean lifetime of 2.2 μs (proper) are produced 15 km above the ground and travel downwards at 0.995c. (a) Calculate γ. (b) Calculate the mean lifetime in Earth’s frame and the mean distance travelled before decay. (c) Calculate the thickness of the atmosphere in the muon frame. (d) Explain why many muons are detected at sea level, although without relativity hardly any would be.
items.answer: (a) γ = 10.0; (b) 22 μs, 0.995 × 3 × 10⁸ × 22 × 10⁻⁶ = 6.6 km; (c) 15/10 = 1.5 km; (d) the travel time (50 μs in Earth frame) is about 2.3 dilated lifetimes, so e^(−2.3) ≈ 10 % survive, rather than e^(−23) without relativity.

items.stem: "The twin paradox shows that special relativity is self-contradictory." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: There is no contradiction: the asymmetry of the journeys explains why the travelling twin ages less.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each twin sees the other’s clock run slow, which appears symmetric. Arguments against: the travelling twin changes inertial frames (accelerates) when turning round, so the situation is not symmetric; space-time diagrams show the travelling twin’s path has a shorter proper time; experiments with atomic clocks on aircraft confirm the asymmetry. Supported judgement: There is no contradiction: the asymmetry of the journeys explains why the travelling twin ages less. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Hana is revising time dilation, length contraction and relativistic velocity addition. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The Lorentz factor can be less than 1 for slow-moving objects.
The clock works perfectly in its own frame; the time dilation is a property of measurements made from another frame.
Relativity says that everything is relative, including the speed of light.
The x′ and ct′ axes of a moving frame are perpendicular on the S diagram.
items.answer: The clock works perfectly in its own frame; the time dilation is a property of measurements made from another frame.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. The clock works perfectly in its own frame; the time dilation is a property of measurements made from another frame.

items.stem: Sofia travels from Earth to Tau Ceti (11.9 ly in Earth’s frame) at 0.95c. Calculate the journey time in years measured by Sofia’s clock.
items.answer: 3.91 years

items.stem: Which quantity is invariant under the Lorentz transformation?
items.answer: The spacetime interval

items.stem: Distinguish between a timelike interval and a spacelike interval.
items.answer: A timelike interval ((cΔt)² > Δx²) can connect cause and effect and has the same time order in all frames; a spacelike interval (Δx² > (cΔt)²) cannot be bridged by any signal, and the time order of the events depends on the frame.
items.markingKey: A timelike interval ((cΔt)² > Δx²) can connect cause and effect and has the same time order in all frames; a spacelike interval (Δx² > (cΔt)²) cannot be bridged by any signal, and the time order of the events depends on the frame. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).
